summary: This document describes a simple way to encapsulate SCTP packets in UDP packets, and its limitations. This lets SCTP work across legacy NATs that do not support it. It also lets applications implement SCTP without direct IP-layer access or special privileges.

plainLanguage.summary: Some network gear does not understand SCTP packets. Putting them inside ordinary UDP envelopes lets them get through.

subtitle: Wrapping SCTP packets in UDP so they cross legacy NATs and can run in applications without special privileges.

tldr.problem: SCTP runs directly over IP, so legacy NATs without SCTP support block it, and user processes usually need special privileges to reach the IP layer.
tldr.mechanism: A UDP header is inserted between the IP header and the SCTP common header, normally using UDP port 9899 on both ends, with rules for ports, checksums, ICMP, path MTU and addresses.
tldr.outcome: SCTP can work through legacy NATs and be built into applications. The RFC was later updated by RFC 8899, and it covers only end-hosts, not tunnel endpoints.

facts.label: Path MTU change
facts.value: Decrease by the UDP header size when encapsulating

today: RFC 6951 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 8899. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Put SCTP Inside UDP
sections.content:
SCTP, defined in RFC 4960, runs directly over IPv4 or IPv6. This RFC describes a simple method of encapsulating SCTP packets in UDP packets. There are two main reasons: to let SCTP traffic pass through legacy NATs that do not provide native SCTP support, and to let SCTP be implemented on hosts that give no direct access to the IP layer, so an application can bring its own SCTP stack.

SCTP still supplies the congestion control and reliability that UDP does not. The document covers only end-hosts, not tunneling endpoints. It also does not say how to find out whether the peer uses UDP encapsulation, or which remote UDP port to use; those are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP is the careful messenger. UDP is a plain envelope that every post office accepts. The careful messenger just rides inside the plain envelope.

sections.title: Use Cases and UNSAF
sections.content:
The first use case is portable SCTP implementations. Some operating systems lack a kernel SCTP stack, or need special privileges to install one, and most require privileges for a user process to touch the IP layer. UDP encapsulation lets SCTP live in a user process with no special privileges. A crucial point there is controlling the source address of outgoing packets.

The second is legacy NAT traversal. For single-homed associations, IP addresses MUST NOT be listed in the INIT and INIT-ACK chunks. To use several addresses, the dynamic address reconfiguration extension (RFC 5061) MUST be used only with wildcard addresses in ASCONF chunks, together with RFC 4895. SCTP sends periodic HEARTBEAT chunks on idle paths, which can keep NAT state alive.

Because RFC 3424 (UNSAF) requires a limited scope, the document covers only endpoints dealing with these legacy constraints. Its stated exit strategy is hosts and middleboxes that support SCTP natively.
sections.plainLanguage: Some places will not let SCTP in, and some programs are not allowed to send it directly. Using UDP gets around both problems.

sections.title: Ports and Architecture
sections.content:
UDP-encapsulated SCTP normally uses the IANA-assigned UDP port 9899 (sctp-tunneling) on both ends. Other ports may be needed, for example by stacks inside applications, and NATs may change port numbers, so the receiver can see ports different from those the sender used. Discovering alternate ports is out of scope.

Each SCTP stack uses a single local UDP encapsulation port as the destination port for all its incoming SCTP packets. That is not strictly required, but it simplifies design. It is not possible if the stack is part of each application, there are several applications, and some want the same IP address.

An implementation MUST keep a remote UDP encapsulation port per destination address for each association, because NAT remapping can make the remote ports for different addresses differ even for the same stack. Implementations need APIs to set other port numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side has a normal door number, 9899, but may use another door. So each address you write to gets its own remembered door number.

sections.title: The Packet Format
sections.content: To encapsulate an SCTP packet, a UDP header (RFC 768) is inserted between the IP header (RFC 791) and the SCTP common header. For IPv4 the order is the IPv4 header, UDP header, SCTP common header, then SCTP chunks 1 to n. For IPv6 the order is the IPv6 base header, extension headers 1 to m (m can be 0), UDP header, SCTP common header, then the chunks.
sections.plainLanguage: The plain UDP envelope goes on the outside, right before the SCTP envelope and the letters inside it.

sections.title: Encapsulation and Decapsulation
sections.content:
When sending, the UDP source port MUST be the stack's local UDP encapsulation port. The destination port MUST be the remote encapsulation port kept for that association and destination address. The UDP length MUST be the SCTP packet length plus the size of the UDP header. The SCTP checksum MUST be computed for IPv4 and IPv6, and the UDP checksum SHOULD be computed for both. The RFC does not specify a zero UDP checksum mode for IPv6, noting that deployed support may be limited and that it would run against the goal of legacy NAT traversal.

When receiving, the UDP header is removed and the usual SCTP lookup finds the association, including the verification tag check. Only then MUST the UDP source port be stored as the encapsulation port for the address the packet came from. If a non-encapsulated SCTP packet arrives, encapsulation of outgoing packets for that association and address MUST be disabled.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing: put your door number and the other side's door number on the outer envelope. Reading: open the outer envelope, check the inner one is really for you, then remember which door it came from.

sections.title: ICMP, MTU, Addresses and ECN
sections.content:
ICMP. An ICMP or ICMPv6 message that cannot be tied to a specific association, or whose verification tag cannot be checked, MUST be discarded silently, and a stack MUST NOT rely on receiving them. If processed, ICMP Port Unreachable SHOULD be treated as Protocol Unreachable, and ICMPv6 Port Unreachable SHOULD be treated as Parameter Problem with code 'unrecognized Next Header type encountered'.

Path MTU. An endpoint that starts encapsulating a path MUST decrease its Path MTU by the size of the UDP header, and SHOULD increase it again if it stops. Path MTU discovery cannot rely on ICMP feedback, and if the DF bit cannot be controlled, an implementation-specific value should be used.

Embedded addresses. For legacy NAT traversal, IP addresses that might need translation MUST NOT go in any SCTP packet. A multihomed association starts single-homed and other addresses are added via RFC 5061 with wildcard addresses only. An ABORT with the T-bit set MAY indicate that the addresses seen by the peer changed.

ECN. If ECN bits are supported, they MUST NOT be changed during sending and receiving.

An informational socket API section adds one read/write option, SCTP_REMOTE_UDP_ENCAPS_PORT, with a structure holding an association id, an address and a port. A port value of 0 disables UDP encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: A few extra rules cover lost-letter notices, the thinner room left in the envelope, hiding home addresses and keeping traffic warning flags unchanged.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encapsulating SCTP in UDP adds no security considerations beyond those of RFC 4960 and RFC 5061. Firewalls that inspect SCTP packets must also know about the encapsulation and apply matching rules to encapsulated packets.

An attacker might send a malicious UDP packet to change the encapsulation port for one remote address of an association. As Section 5.4 specifies, that requires one of the two negotiated verification tags, which protects against blind attackers as RFC 4960 describes for SCTP over IPv4 or IPv6. Non-blind attackers can affect an association in the same way as with unencapsulated SCTP.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster cannot easily change which door you use, because they would need the secret code both sides agreed on.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document refers to the already assigned UDP port 9899 (sctp-tunneling), and IANA updated the assignment to refer to this RFC. The TCP port 9899 assignment is no longer needed, so IANA removed it and marked TCP port 9899 as Reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: The number-keeper confirmed door 9899 is for this, and closed the matching door on the other road.
